titre: The Shroud of Turin, a Fraud Already Denounced in 1389
accroche: In 1988, three laboratories date the linen of the Shroud of Turin to between 1260 and 1390: a range that contains a bishop's denunciation in 1389.
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 1355, in the small collegiate church of Lirey, in Champagne, a linen cloth bearing the imprint of a tortured body began to be shown to pilgrims: that, it was said, of Christ taken down from the cross. About thirty years later, the bishop of the diocese, Pierre d'Arcis, wrote to the antipope Clement VII, in Avignon, to ask that the exhibition be banned. His 1389 memorandum leaves no room for ambiguity: the cloth had been painted “skillfully,” and the artist who painted it had himself admitted to having made it by human hand.

## A Relic Judged Twice

Clement VII decides halfway: the exhibition may continue, on condition of announcing publicly that it is not the “true shroud of Our Lord Jesus Christ,” only a painting made to represent it. It was in 1506 that Pope Julius II reversed the decision and authorized the faithful who believe it authentic to venerate it as such. The shroud has been in Turin since 1578.

In 1988, after years of discussions to obtain the agreement of the Holy See, radiocarbon dating was carried out by three laboratories: Oxford, Arizona, and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich. Published in the journal Nature in 1989, the results establish that the linen dates, with 95% confidence, from the years 1260 to 1390. This range encompasses the first exhibition at Lirey, around 1355, and the memorandum of the bishop of Troyes, in 1389.

## What This Shifts

The shroud therefore did not wait for the 20th century and chemistry to be doubted: a 14th-century bishop, who claimed to have it from an artist's admission that he had painted the cloth, had already maintained that the cloth was the work of an artist, and the 1988 dating places the linen in the 13th-14th century, not in the time of Christ. In between, Rome ended up authorizing the veneration of the shroud. Defenders of its authenticity have since put forward that an invisible medieval repair would have skewed the sample taken in 1988; these hypotheses have since been examined and refuted one by one by other researchers.

What the episode shifts is therefore not only a date: it is the idea that a rigorous doubt about a relic would be a modern invention, set against a uniform medieval credulity. Here, it is a 14th-century bishop who raised the doubt, and Rome that afterward authorized veneration.

citation.texte: The shroud was painted skillfully, and it was proven by the artist who painted it that it was made by human hand, and not miraculously produced.

carte.punch: 1988: radiocarbon dates the shroud to 1260-1390, the time when a bishop had denounced it.
carte.idee: In 1389, the bishop of Troyes denounces the Shroud of Turin as a painting, backed by an artist's admission. Rome authorizes its veneration in 1506. In 1988, three laboratories date the linen by radiocarbon to between 1260 and 1390: a range that contains the Lirey exhibition and the 1389 memorandum.

quiz.question: What does the 1988 dating show with regard to the history of the shroud?
choix: Because it confirms that the shroud does date from the 1st century, contrary to expectations
That the linen dates from the years 1260 to 1390, a range that contains the bishop of Troyes's denunciation in 1389
Because it was carried out by a single laboratory, with no possibility of verification
Because it immediately convinced all the defenders of the shroud's authenticity
quiz.explication: The 1260-1390 range encompasses the exhibition at Lirey (around 1355) and Pierre d'Arcis's memorandum (1389): it therefore does not point to an ancient origin. Three laboratories dated the cloth, and defenders of authenticity challenged the result afterward, hypotheses since refuted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Bishop Pierre d'Arcis's memorandum, written in 1389, say about the shroud?
choix: That it was painted skillfully, the artist himself having admitted it
That it is beyond any doubt the true shroud of Christ
That it was stolen from a monastery in Jerusalem by crusaders
That it must be destroyed immediately to avoid a scandal
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pierre d'Arcis writes that the cloth was painted skillfully and that the artist who painted it had admitted to making it by human hand; he does not authenticate it, mentions no theft, and asks only for the exhibition to be banned, not for its destruction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Pope Julius II decide in 1506 about the shroud?
choix: He confirms the total ban on any exhibition of the shroud
He authorizes the faithful who believe it authentic to venerate it as such
He orders a new canonical inquiry into the origin of the cloth
He transfers the shroud from Lirey to Jerusalem
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Julius II reverses in 1506 the decision of Clement VII, which allowed the exhibition only with a public announcement denying its authenticity, and from then on permits the faithful to venerate the shroud as authentic; no canonical inquiry or transfer to Jerusalem is mentioned.
